title: The only fair ruler, and how far apart two worlds can be

data.source: Chentsov (1972); Bhattacharyya (1943); Myers (1941). Numerical check on the worked circle of Phoenix_Egg/CORE/MATHEMATICS.md and on 160000 random pairs of distributions, seeded.

prediction: R1 is the Fisher metric, so the worked circle keeps its length 2.794018 when outcomes are split, loses length when outcomes are merged, the simplex distance 0.880169 is the Bhattacharyya angle, and the greatest distance between any two distributions is pi, half the Bonnet-Myers bound.
baseline: Chentsov's uniqueness theorem (1972), the Bhattacharyya angle (1943) and Myers' diameter theorem (1941).
why: All five statements held. R1 (status ASSUMPTION in Phoenix) is Chentsov's metric with its one free constant given to sigma; the number pi is the diameter of every probability simplex in the usual units and pi/2 in the other common units. The owner's wider claim that Bonnet-Myers is "saturated" holds for qubit pure states but not for classical distributions, where the diameter is half the bound. Chentsov's theorem gives no circle, no cut and no ruler size; those remain choices.
